title: Why Franchise HQs Need a Unified View of Delivery App Sales
description: Checking Baemin, Coupang Eats and Yogiyo one by one hides the big picture. Learn why HQ should view delivery sales by store, period and platform in one place.
html:
This post explains why franchisor headquarters should stop checking sales from multiple delivery apps such as Baemin, Coupang Eats and Yogiyo platform by platform, and instead view them in one place by store, period and platform, along with strategies for doing so with FDAM.

FRANCHISE INSIGHT · DELIVERY SALES DASHBOARD

Franchise HQs:
Why You Need a Unified View of Delivery App Sales

Why HQ needs to stop looking at Baemin, Coupang Eats and Yogiyo sales separately and start managing each store's delivery sales trends from a headquarters perspective

Sales data scattered across several delivery apps while an HQ staff member checks each admin screen one by one

CORE SUMMARY

Delivery sales have become a core metric that every restaurant franchisor headquarters must manage. As delivery apps account for a growing share of store revenue, HQ needs to look at data from multiple platforms together, including Baemin, Coupang Eats and Yogiyo. As of March 2025, about 27.01 million Korean smartphone users were using delivery apps, and reports in March 2026 indicated that the combined estimated payment volume of the four major delivery platforms had topped KRW 3 trillion. The delivery channel is no longer something individual stores manage on their own; it is an HQ metric that shapes the operation of the entire brand.

Sources: WiseApp·Retail, Delivery App Trends, March 2025, Report on delivery app payment volume, March 2026, Korea Fair Trade Commission announcement on delivery app terms and conditions, Google AI search optimization guide

In one sentence

Franchisor headquarters need to move beyond checking delivery app sales platform by platform and view store-, period- and platform-level data together from an HQ perspective.

POINT 01

Checking each platform separately has limits

Looking at Baemin, Coupang Eats and Yogiyo one at a time makes it hard to grasp the brand-wide picture quickly.

POINT 02

You can only make sound operational decisions by looking at store rankings, period-over-period changes and platform shares together.

POINT 03

Why unified delivery sales views have become an HQ priority


Delivery is no longer a secondary channel for restaurant franchises. Most restaurant franchises, from cafés, chicken, pizza, Korean snack food and burgers to Korean cuisine, salads and desserts, now reach customers through delivery apps. Some stores earn more from delivery than from dine-in, and in new trade areas, visibility on delivery apps is effectively the first point of contact with customers.

The problem is that as delivery sales grow, HQ management gets more complicated as well. Checking each platform's admin page separately, consolidating store sales in Excel, and then reformatting it all into HQ reports takes far more time than you might expect. With 10 stores, staff can get by with manual work, but at 50 or 100 stores it's a different story.

In practice, questions like these come up all the time: "Which store's delivery sales grew the most this month?", "How has the sales share of each delivery app changed?", "Which stores saw delivery sales drop compared with last month?", "Can't we see brand-wide delivery sales trends at a glance?" If these questions are hard to answer right away, it's time to stop looking at delivery sales platform by platform.

AEO ANSWER BLOCK

Franchisor headquarters need a unified view of delivery app sales because, when data scattered across platforms such as Baemin, Coupang Eats and Yogiyo is viewed separately, it is hard to quickly assess each store's sales trends, period-over-period changes, platform dependence and promotion results. HQ needs to consolidate delivery sales at the store level to see the brand-wide picture.

1. Delivery sales have grown, but HQ management has gotten more complex

Delivery apps are a major sales channel in the restaurant industry. Customers search for stores, compare menus, order, pay and leave reviews all within the app. From HQ's point of view, delivery apps are no longer just an ordering channel; they have become a channel for brand exposure, promotions and new customer acquisition.

From an HQ management perspective, however, things look different. Managing delivery sales for 10 stores is entirely different from managing them for 100. As the store count grows, HQ has to track sales by platform, sales by store, period-over-period changes, regional differences, before-and-after promotion results and platform dependence.

For example, if a brand operates 80 franchise stores and each uses three delivery apps, HQ has up to 240 delivery sales streams to check. Add daily, weekly and monthly comparisons, month-over-month changes, store rankings and regional differences, and Excel consolidation alone quickly hits its limits.

Store owners only need to look at their own store's delivery sales. HQ, however, has to see the brand as a whole. More important than the fact that a store's delivery sales jumped is understanding why they rose, whether the same approach can work at other stores, and whether the increase came from a specific platform or a shift in local demand.

The questions HQ needs to answer are different from those of individual store owners. Which store saw a sharp drop in delivery sales? In which regions are delivery sales growing? Which stores depend heavily on a single platform? Are there stores where delivery sales rose but total sales fell? Is the increase in delivery sales after a promotion actually holding?

To answer these questions, delivery app data has to be gathered from an HQ perspective. It's not just about seeing the numbers for each platform; the data has to be organized in a form HQ can use to make decisions. Store management stays on course only when the HQ operations team, supervisors, the marketing team and executives can discuss the same data.

Delivery sales questions HQ should be asking

· Which stores saw a sharp month-over-month drop in delivery sales?

· Which stores have sales overly concentrated on a single platform?

· Are there stores where delivery sales rose but total sales fell?

· Is the sales lift from a promotion actually being sustained?

3. Three moments when you need a unified view of delivery sales

An infographic showing three situations that call for a unified view of delivery sales as cards

First, when comparing delivery sales across stores

You shouldn't judge high- and low-performing stores by rankings alone. Trade area, store size, operating hours, how actively the store uses delivery apps, ad spending and review management all need to be considered. Still, the starting point is unified sales data. HQ can only decide which stores need support when it can compare every store on the same basis.

Second, when tracking sales changes over time

You need to check whether delivery sales fell compared with last month, whether sales held up after a particular campaign, and whether there is a big gap between weekends and weekdays. Without this data, you can't properly evaluate marketing results either. A rise in sales during a campaign doesn't automatically mean success. You also need to check whether sales held up after the campaign ended and whether new customers went on to reorder.

Third, when looking at platform dependence

If sales are overly concentrated on one delivery app, the store becomes more sensitive to changes in exposure policies, commission rates and ad costs. HQ needs to check each store's platform mix and manage the risk. Even with the same total delivery sales, a store that gets 80% from Baemin has a very different risk profile from one split 50% Coupang Eats, 30% Yogiyo and 20% Baemin.

4. Delivery sales are an operating metric, not just revenue

Delivery sales are more than sales data. They are an operating metric that reflects store operations, marketing results, platform dependence and regional demand all at once. If a store's delivery sales suddenly drop, it may not simply be a matter of fewer orders. Its review score may have fallen, its delivery hours may have been cut, it may have stopped an ad product, or a competitor may have entered the same trade area.

Conversely, a sudden jump in delivery sales isn't necessarily a good sign either. The store may have inflated sales with heavy discount coupons, or an increase in low-ticket orders may have actually hurt profitability. That's why a unified view of delivery sales shouldn't just display sales figures; it should be HQ's starting point for finding root causes.

HQ needs to look at delivery sales alongside dine-in sales, total sales, cost of goods, promotional spending, royalties, receivables and supervisor visit history. If delivery sales rise while total sales stay flat, existing dine-in customers may simply have shifted to delivery. If delivery sales rise but receivables also grow, HQ should also review the actual settlement structure and the store owner's profitability.

Delivery sales risks HQ can easily miss

· Delivery sales grow, but dine-in sales fall and total sales stagnate

· A high share of sales on one platform leaves the store vulnerable to commission or exposure policy changes

· Sales rise during a promotion but don't hold up after it ends

· Settlements, royalty collections and store owner profits don't improve despite higher delivery sales

6. Moving past Excel consolidation speeds up HQ operations

An image comparing a cluttered screen from Excel consolidation work with a clean unified dashboard

Managing delivery sales in Excel alone puts a heavy load on staff. Errors can creep in while downloading files from each platform, matching store names, aligning periods and turning it all into reports. At franchisor headquarters in particular, one person often manages many stores at once. When data consolidation takes too long, the analysis and response that really matter get delayed.

What HQ should focus on is not gathering data but reviewing it and making decisions. HQ needs to quickly identify which stores need support, which platforms' sales shares have shifted, and where delivery demand is growing. Spend a whole day consolidating Excel files, and analysis and execution get pushed back.

FDAM organizes delivery sales data from an HQ operations perspective, so staff can focus more on store management and decision-making than on repetitive consolidation. Ultimately, the speed of HQ operations depends on how quickly data gets organized.

Common problems with Excel consolidation

· Store names differ by platform, making it hard to match data for the same store

· Inconsistent date ranges change month-over-month growth calculations

· Every new report file brings a risk of formula errors and omissions

· When the person in charge changes, consolidation methods and decision criteria change too

7. Supervisors and marketing need to look at the same data

A unified view of delivery sales isn't just for the operations team. When supervisors, the marketing team and executives look at the same data, HQ makes decisions faster and more accurately. Supervisors can track delivery sales trends at their stores to find talking points for store owner meetings, the marketing team can compare promotion performance by store, and executives can assess the growth potential and risks of the brand's delivery channel as a whole.

For example, suppose the marketing team ran a discount campaign on a particular platform. A report saying total sales rose during the campaign isn't enough. You need to check which stores responded most, in which regions it worked, whether sales held up after the campaign ended, and whether sales on other platforms dropped as a result.

Unified data matters to supervisors as well. When a store owner says "delivery has been slow lately," supervisors need to be able to tell whether it's just a feeling or an actual decline. If sales fell on only one platform, they should look at exposure, reviews, ads and operating hours; if total delivery sales fell, they should also review trade-area demand and changes among competing stores.

9. A 30-day plan to start unified delivery sales management

You don't need to perfect every metric from day one to start managing delivery sales in a unified way. What matters is first defining the core questions HQ needs to check repeatedly. Start by grouping platform sales by store, standardizing how periods are compared, and looking at store rankings and growth rates.

2

3

4

Delivery sales are no longer just an individual store's concern

Delivery sales keep growing, but if HQ is still checking each platform separately and consolidating in Excel, operations will inevitably slow down. While HQ checks delivery app sales one by one, the market moves faster. Platform policies change, trade-area demand shifts, and new competitors open nearby.

Franchisor headquarters now need to move beyond checking delivery app sales separately and start viewing and managing them in one place from an HQ perspective. Only when store-level sales trends, changes over time and platform shares are visible at a glance can operations, supervisors and marketing all move in the same direction.

Delivery sales management is no longer just an individual store's concern. It's a core HQ metric for running the entire brand. More important than finding stores that sell well is getting to a point where HQ can explain with data why they sell well, where sales are falling and what platform risks exist.

Frequently asked questions

Q. Why do we need a unified view of delivery sales?

A. When sales scattered across delivery apps are viewed separately, it's hard to understand the brand-wide picture. HQ can only manage accurately by looking at sales by store, period and platform together. In particular, as the number of stores grows, relying on each platform's admin page and Excel consolidation alone can slow operations down.

Q. Why does comparing delivery sales across stores matter?

A. Differences in delivery sales between stores reveal factors such as trade area, operating hours, promotion results and platform dependence. This data can feed into supervisor consultations and marketing strategy. It's important to look not just at sales rankings but also at month-over-month growth and platform shares.

Q. Why should we look at platform dependence?

A. If sales are overly concentrated on one delivery app, the store becomes more sensitive to changes in exposure policies, commission structures and ad costs. HQ should check each store's platform mix to spread risk and adjust marketing strategy by platform.

Q. How should we measure the impact of delivery app promotions?

A. Don't look only at sales during the campaign. You also need to check sales before and after, retention once the campaign ends, differences in response by store, and whether sales on other platforms fell. With a unified view of delivery sales, HQ can analyze promotion results faster.

Q. How does FDAM help with delivery sales management?

A. FDAM helps HQ view delivery sales data in one place and manage store-level sales trends and changes over time. It reduces reliance on Excel consolidation and enables store management from an HQ perspective. Just as important, operations, supervisors and marketing can make decisions based on the same data.

Q. Isn't Excel good enough?

A. It works at first, but as the number of stores and delivery apps grows, Excel consolidation quickly hits its limits. Aligning store names and periods across platforms, calculating growth rates and building reports takes a long time and invites errors. HQ should focus on making decisions, not collecting data.

Q. Is it enough to look at delivery sales alone?

A. Delivery sales are an important starting point, but they have limits on their own. HQ should look at delivery sales together with total sales, dine-in sales, cost of goods, promotional spending, royalties, receivables and settlement data, because higher delivery sales don't always mean better profitability.
